answers_by_date.basis: The starting answer is No and nothing changed between 2000 and 2020 to explain a different answer. Ley 22.439 (in force until January 2004) had no provision on employers holding migrants' documents. Ley 17.671, art. 14 (1968, unamended) already said the DNI 'no podrá ser retenido a su titular' except by listed authorities; see starting_answer_concern. No practice evidence was gathered because the protection answer is the lowest option.

Ley 25.871 (in force from January 2004) has no clause against confiscating documents; its documents chapter (arts. 30-33) only governs who may obtain a DNI. Ley 17.671, art. 14 was unchanged. No relevant event.

Ley 26.364 on trafficking (2008) entered into force. Its art. 6 guarantees victims documentation to stay in the country, but it does not prohibit holding identity documents. Decreto 616/2010 (May 2010) came after this date and its art. 30 only concerns the DNI procedure. Answer unchanged.

Ley 26.842 (December 2012) replaced art. 2 and art. 6 of Ley 26.364 but added no ban on retaining documents. Ley 17.671, art. 14 was unchanged. Answer unchanged. Practice context: CMW/C/ARG/CO/1 (2011), para. 21, found irregular migrants in the textile, agriculture and domestic-work sectors subject to forced labour and to 'restrictions on their freedom of movement'. It does not mention documents.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

answers.repealed_search: I looked for a protection that existed between 2000 and 2020 and was later repealed. I read Ley 22.439 (the Ley Videla), arts. 98-105, the documents chapter of Ley 25.871 and its antecedentes normativos, Decreto 616/2010 art. 30, and Ley 26.364 as amended by Ley 26.842. None of them prohibited, or later dropped a prohibition on, confiscating migrants' documents. The only rule found on withholding documents is Ley 17.671, art. 14. It has been in force without change since 1968 and was never repealed.

practice_sources.title: CMW, Concluding observations on Argentina, CMW/C/ARG/CO/1

answers.sourcing_note: The current texts were read on InfoLEG together with their amendment notes. Ley 22.439 was read in its final consolidated text. Decreto 1023/94 was not read. The answer is No on every date, so the dating does not affect it.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The No may be wrong, at least for migrants who hold a DNI. Ley 17.671, art. 14 (1968, no amendment note on InfoLEG) covers every person domiciled in Argentina (art. 1), which includes permanent and temporary foreign residents with a DNI. It says the DNI 'no podrá ser retenido a su titular, salvo' by the authority to which it is shown when it appears illegitimately held, by the trial court, by military authorities, by asylum and hospice authorities, or by legal representatives of persons lacking capacity. That is close to a ban on confiscation by anyone except authorised officials. It does not reach passports or foreign identity documents, and it carries no criminal penalty for an employer. This rule was in force on every date from 2000 to 2020, so it would change the answer on all dates, not just one.
answers.notes: The answer stays No on every date, following the starting answer. No rulings were relied on. CP art. 294 (destroying or suppressing a document) and CP art. 140 (servitude) might reach some cases of document retention, but neither is a specific right against confiscation.

answers_by_date.basis: Birth registration was governed by Decreto-Ley 8204/63 (ratified by Ley 16.478), which required registration of all births in the national territory whatever the parents' status, and by Ley 24.540 (1995) on identifying newborns. Constitution art. 20 and Ley 346 (ius soli) also applied. I could not open the text of 8204/63; Ley 26.413, art. 27(a), which replaced it, keeps the same rule. I found no practice evidence specific to migrants for this period, so the rating is inferred.
Same regime as in 2000 (Decreto-Ley 8204/63 and Ley 24.540). Ley 25.871 came into force in 2004 and does not restrict registration. No migrant-specific practice evidence for this period.

Ley 26.413 (published 6 October 2008, in force about 14 October 2008) replaced Decreto-Ley 8204/63 (art. 95). Its art. 27(a) requires registration of 'Todos los que ocurran en el territorio de la Nación', with ex officio registration after 40 days (art. 28). Ley 26.061, arts. 12-13 (October 2005) also requires free, immediate identification of newborns even when parents have no documents. CRC/C/ARG/CO/3-4 (2010) welcomed free, universal, ex officio registration but noted insufficient implementation in the provinces.

Ley 26.413, arts. 27-29 (original 2008 text) and Ley 26.061, arts. 12-13 were in force and unamended; art. 27 was only replaced by Ley 27.611 in January 2021. I found no practice evidence from around 2015. The rating sits between the gaps the CRC documented in 2010 and the starting rating for 2020.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.sourcing_note: I read the original 2008 text of Ley 26.413 and its current text with amendment notes. I could not open Decreto-Ley 8204/63 or Ley 24.540 (the PDF and the Buenos Aires City page failed), so the 2000 and 2005 answers rest on the repeal clause in Ley 26.413 and on secondary indications. The CRC 2010 evidence concerns children generally (indigenous, poor and remote children) rather than migrants specifically.

answers.starting_answer_concern: The answer holds. The 'Effectively Always' rating is generous given the CRC's 2010 and 2018 concerns about under-registration, but I found no migrant-specific evidence of refusals.
answers.notes: Ley 26.413, art. 27 was replaced by Ley 27.611 (B.O. 15/01/2021), after 1 January 2020, so the 2020 answer rests on the original 2008 text quoted above. The implementation ratings for 2000 and 2005 are inferred.

answers_by_date.basis: Under Ley 22.439, art. 98 only foreigners authorised as permanent residents could obtain the DNI; under art. 99 temporary residents could do so only if their residence was for one year or more. Art. 100 required the DNI to state nationality, type of residence, the file and the expiry date. Ley 17.671, arts. 1 and 11 had RENAPER issue DNIs to all persons domiciled in Argentina. I found no practice evidence from this period; the rating reflects the restrictive regime and widespread irregularity and is low confidence.

Ley 25.871 (in force from January 2004), art. 30, lets permanent and temporary residents obtain the DNI. Art. 31 covers recognised refugees, art. 32 sets the DNI's term to that of temporary residence, and art. 33 requires it to state nationality, type of residence, resolution and term. Precarious residence was available pending a decision. Ley 25.871 was not yet regulated, and the large backlog of irregular migrants was only addressed by the Patria Grande programme from 2006.

Same provisions as in 2005; Decreto 616/2010, art. 30 (DNI procedure) came in May 2010, after this date. CMW/C/ARG/CO/1 (2011) records that Patria Grande granted residence to 'more than half' of 423,711 applicants, so the backlog was being reduced but with significant gaps.

Ley 25.871, arts. 30-33 (unamended) and Decreto 616/2010, art. 30 required the migration authority to notify RENAPER and set a 60-day period to apply for the DNI. DNU 70/2017 (from January 2017) did not touch arts. 30-33. I read no practice report from around 2015, so the rating is inferred from the 2011 CMW findings.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but they are not the same

answers.sourcing_note: Ley 22.439 (final text) and Ley 25.871 with its full list of amendments were read on InfoLEG. Arts. 30-33 have no amendment notes. Decreto 1023/94 was not read. I found no practice evidence for 2000, 2005 or 2015; CELS and CMW 2019 PDFs could not be opened. The 2000, 2005 and 2015 ratings are inferred.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The Yes holds for residence status and identity, since the DNI must state the type and term of residence. Work status is not stated on the DNI; it follows from the residence category. The 2020 rating 'Usually; Effectively Always' may be high: CELS reported large fee increases in 2018 and RaDEX-related disruption in 2019, but I could not open those reports.
answers.notes: The scale option 'not the same' was chosen because the DNI rule widened in 2004 (all temporary residents, plus refugees). Implementation also improved over the period.

answers_by_date.basis: Código Penal art. 294 penalises anyone who suppresses or destroys a document, in whole or in part, in a way that may cause harm. It has no amendment note and was in force on this date. It covers DNIs and residence documents of any holder. No practice evidence found; the rating follows the starting answer.
CP art. 294 unchanged. The art. 292 penalties it refers to for identity documents were set by Ley 24.410 (1995). Ley 25.890 (2004) added art. 293 bis, which is not relevant. No practice evidence.
CP art. 294 unchanged. No practice evidence specific to migrants.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

provisions.article: Arts. 292, 297 (penalties and equivalences referred to by art. 294; as replaced by Ley 24.410, B.O. 2/1/1995)

answers.sourcing_note: The consolidated Código Penal on InfoLEG shows no amendment note on art. 294; the arts. 292-293 notes date from 1995 (Ley 24.410), before the period. I found no practice evidence on prosecutions for destroying migrants' documents, so the implementation ratings are not supported by evidence.
answers.notes: Art. 294 reads: 'El que suprimiere o destruyere, en todo o en parte, un documento de modo que pueda resultar perjuicio, incurrirá en las penas señaladas en los artículos anteriores'. It is a general offence, not specific to migrants. No amendment between 2000 and 2020 affected it.
